speaker: Kelsey Hightower
title: Kubernetes and retiring at the top with Kelsey Hightower
question: In cloud infrastructure, why does letting an AI agent directly manage a raw cloud console fail in practice?
guest: Everyone says, 'I don't need Terraform, I'm just going to use an AI agent to manage the cloud.' Having seen what humans do when you just give them the raw AWS console, watch what an agent is going to do with it. If you point these agents directly at the console, they just start investigating services—trying a Lambda function, deciding they don't need it, trying a load balancer, deciding they don't need it—except those resources are now running and the agent doesn't even know the mess it made. Instead of pointing the agent at all of AWS, you need a context engine so it only queries the specific resources your team actually uses. You also need the same guardrails and infrastructure-as-code structure that the rest of your system relies on, so the agent interacts with the platform the same way humans and pipelines do. We're not asking the agent to be magic; we're asking it to be an alternative interface on top of existing structure and guardrails.

points.core: Exploratory agents spin up orphaned cloud resources without tracking the resulting mess.
points.note: Accept: agents try and abandon services like functions or load balancers, leaving untracked running infrastructure or hidden costs. Do not credit: generic mentions of 'AI hallucinations' or 'security risks'.

points.core: Unscoped console access exposes irrelevant services instead of resources the team uses.
points.note: Accept: lack of a bounded context engine limiting the agent to the organization's actual resource footprint. Do not credit: generic advice to 'give better prompts'.

points.core: Reliable agents act as an interface over existing deterministic platform guardrails.
points.note: Accept: routing agent actions through existing IaC or platform APIs and guardrails rather than raw cloud consoles. Do not credit: vague advice to 'keep a human in the loop'.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
It fails because a raw cloud console is an imperative, stateful, high-blast-radius interface, and agents are probabilistic operators that need the opposite.

A console or raw API exposes thousands of low-level actions with no built-in notion of intent, review, or undo. An agent clicking or calling its way through them produces changes that aren't recorded as code, so there is no diff to review, no plan to preview, and no clean rollback. Small errors, such as a misread resource ID, a hallucinated parameter, or a stale view of current state, become real outages, deleted data, security holes, or runaway bills.

The agent also lacks context the console doesn't show: why resources exist, what depends on them, and which organisational policies apply. Permissions make this worse, since doing useful work requires broad IAM rights, which means mistakes or prompt injection can do broad damage. And its actions aren't reproducible or easily auditable, so drift accumulates and nobody can explain the environment afterward.

What works in practice is putting a constrained layer between the agent and the cloud: infrastructure-as-code, plan-then-apply workflows, policy guardrails, least-privilege scoped credentials, and human approval for destructive changes.

points.why: The response attributes runaway bills and drift to errors and unrecorded changes without describing agents creating and abandoning resources that remain running.
The response describes broad access and missing resource context without connecting the failure to exposure to services outside the team’s actual resource footprint.
The response explicitly puts infrastructure-as-code, plan review, and policy enforcement between the agent and the cloud.
quotes: putting a constrained layer between the agent and the cloud

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Letting an AI agent directly operate a raw cloud console fails because consoles are designed for interactive human navigation, not deterministic, auditable state management. First, web UIs and low-level cloud surfaces are sprawling and brittle: dynamic layouts, deeply nested menus, and hundreds of implicit parameters cause multi-step errors to compound, leaving behind orphaned, half-provisioned, or subtly misconfigured resources whenever an agent misreads context or hallucinates. Second, direct console mutations—essentially automated ClickOps—bypass version control, declarative state, and dry-run execution plans. Without a canonical state file or atomic transactions, imperative edits immediately introduce configuration drift, obscure cross-resource dependencies, and make deterministic rollbacks nearly impossible. Finally, raw console access typically requires broad live credentials and applies changes immediately without policy-as-code guardrails, cost caps, or human review gates, turning a single misinterpreted prompt into production outages, security exposures, or runaway spend. In practice, reliable agentic cloud management works only when agents propose changes through constrained abstractions—such as declarative Infrastructure-as-Code pipelines—backed by automated validation, least-privilege execution, and explicit approval gates.

noweb.answer:
Letting an AI agent directly drive a raw cloud console—essentially automating "ClickOps"—fails in practice because web consoles are built for human exploration rather than deterministic, auditable state management. Cloud UIs change frequently, rely on complex asynchronous rendering, and scatter hidden dependencies across multi-step wizards, making GUI automation slow, brittle, and prone to non-atomic partial failures that leave orphaned or misconfigured resources behind.

More fundamentally, mutating live infrastructure directly bypasses the safeguards production environments depend on, including version control, dry-run diffs, idempotency, policy-as-code checks, and peer review. Because AI agents are probabilistic, a single misread screen or hallucinated setting paired with broad console permissions can silently expose networks, trigger runaway costs, or delete stateful data with no clean rollback path, while immediately creating configuration drift from existing Infrastructure-as-Code repositories. Reliable AI-assisted cloud operations instead have agents author declarative code, allowing deterministic pipelines to validate execution plans, enforce least-privilege guardrails, and keep every change reviewable and reversible before anything touches production.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Giving an AI agent direct control of a raw cloud console usually fails because the console is a huge, permissive surface with no guardrails. It was built for humans who carry context the agent doesn't have. Providers like AWS, GCP and Azure expose thousands of loosely documented, interdependent services and settings. An agent working through clicks or raw API calls can't reliably reason about hidden dependencies such as IAM policies, networking, quotas, billing and region constraints. It also can't see side effects before they happen. One wrong call, like an open security group, a deleted volume or a runaway autoscaling group, can cause an outage, a data leak or a big bill, and many of these mistakes can't be undone. There's no plan/diff step, no review, and no single source of truth, so changes drift, can't be reproduced, and are hard to audit or roll back. Agents also hallucinate parameters and lose state across long, multi-step tasks. In practice, the approach that works puts the agent behind an abstraction layer. That means infrastructure as code such as Terraform or Pulumi, narrowly scoped tools, least-privilege credentials, policy checks, dry-run previews and human approval for destructive actions.

noweb.answer: Letting an AI agent directly operate a raw cloud console fails in practice because web consoles are designed for human exploration rather than reliable, safe automation. Console interfaces are brittle, stateful, and constantly changing, filled with hidden defaults, asynchronous modals, and multi-step wizards that cause agents to misread state or click the wrong controls. More fundamentally, console clicks are imperative mutations that bypass Infrastructure as Code, version control, and peer review. Every manual change introduces configuration drift, leaving environments unreproducible and breaking future automated deployments. Raw consoles also lack strong safety rails: they rarely offer reliable plan-and-diff previews, atomic rollbacks, or automated policy checks before execution. If an agent misunderstands a setting or hallucinates a parameter, destructive actions—like exposing a network, misconfiguring IAM permissions, or deleting storage—take effect immediately with weak auditability. Production infrastructure instead requires declarative, API-driven workflows with strict least-privilege boundaries, dry runs, and human-approved change gates.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A raw cloud console gives an AI agent the same controls as an administrator without turning the administrator’s judgment into enforceable rules. The agent has to infer which account and region it’s in, what depends on a resource, whether a change is authorized, and whether it actually succeeded. A timeout can leave the outcome ambiguous, so retrying may create duplicate resources or compound a partial change. With broad permissions, a single wrong assumption can take down production, expose data, or run up costs.

A more reliable setup gives the agent scoped, typed operations that check preconditions and verify outcomes. Infrastructure-as-code plans make proposed changes reviewable, policy checks enforce limits, and approval gates keep high-impact changes under human control.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A raw cloud console gives an AI agent individual controls, but a user’s request usually describes an outcome, such as “cut costs without hurting availability.” The console shows how resources are configured, but it may not reveal which workloads depend on them or why a seemingly idle database exists. An agent can therefore take a valid action that breaks the service.

Execution adds another problem. Cloud changes often finish asynchronously, and a sequence of console clicks can fail halfway through. If the agent loses track of what succeeded, a retry can duplicate a resource or make recovery harder. Broad permissions increase the impact of each mistake.

A more reliable approach gives the agent scoped permissions and lets it propose a reviewable infrastructure change. A deployment system can then check the plan against policy, track what was applied, and verify the outcome.
